title: Shortest paths: from a promising route to a proven distance
attribution: Original directed graphs, questions, distractors and worked explanations for RecallWeave. Algorithm background: MIT OpenCourseWare, 6.006 Introduction to Algorithms (Spring 2020), Erik Demaine, Jason Ku and Justin Solomon, Lectures 11 and 13: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/pages/lecture-notes/. No reference exercise, figure or passage is copied. AI assistance was used in drafting and implementation.

items.prompt: A directed graph has exactly these edges: S → A costs 4, A → T costs 3, and S → T costs 9. Which route from S to T has the smallest total weight?
options: The direct route, with total cost 9
Both routes, because each reaches T
The route through A, with total cost 7
The direct route, because it uses one edge
items.explanation: The two possible routes cost 9 and 4 + 3 = 7. A weighted shortest path minimizes the sum of its edge weights, so S → A → T wins despite using more edges. Reaching the same destination does not make the costs equal.
items.transfer: If the direct edge changed to 6, which route would become cheaper? State the new total, not just the number of edges.

items.prompt: A graph contains only the directed edges S → A with weight 2 and A → T with weight 2. What can you conclude about a route from T back to S?
options: There is no directed route from T to S
T → A → S costs 4 because the edges are reversible
T → S costs 0 because S was the original source
T → A → S costs 2 because only one edge counts
items.explanation: The arrows permit movement from S to A and then to T. They do not provide either reverse edge. From T there is no outgoing edge at all, so S is unreachable from T. Reversing a route is valid only when the needed reverse edges actually exist.
items.transfer: Add the smallest number of directed edges needed to make T able to reach S. Explain why one direct edge is enough.

items.prompt: The only directed edges are S → A with weight 0, A → T with weight 3, and S → T with weight 4. What is the shortest-path cost from S to T?
options: 4 along S → T
0 along S → A
7 by adding every listed edge
3 along S → A → T
items.explanation: S → A → T costs 0 + 3 = 3, which is less than 4. A zero-weight edge is allowed by the nonnegative-weight condition. Stopping at A does not reach T, and a route does not include every edge in the graph.
items.transfer: Does adding a zero-weight edge necessarily create a zero-cost route to every vertex? Give a counterexample using this graph.

items.prompt: In Dijkstra’s algorithm, S has been settled. A has tentative distance 4 and B has tentative distance 1. The directed edge B → A has weight 2. B is settled next. What should relaxing B → A do?
options: Keep A at 4 because its first route was recorded
Set A to 3 and record B as its predecessor
Set A to 2 using only the B → A edge weight
Set A to 1 by copying B’s tentative distance
items.explanation: The new route to A goes through B, so its cost is distance(B) + weight(B → A) = 1 + 2 = 3. Because 3 is below the old estimate 4, the algorithm replaces A’s distance and predecessor. A discovered distance remains tentative until that vertex is settled.
items.transfer: If B → A instead cost 5, would A’s recorded distance or predecessor change? Compare the complete candidate cost with 4.

items.prompt: A fresh Dijkstra run starts at S. The graph contains S, A and T, with edges S → A of weight 3 and A → T of weight 2. Before settling any vertex or relaxing any edge, how should the distance table be initialized?
options: S, A and T all start at 0
S is 0; A is 3; T is 5
S is unreached; A is 3; T is 2
S is 0; A and T are unreached
items.explanation: The empty route from S to itself costs 0. No other route has been explored yet, so A and T start unreached, conventionally written as infinity. A distance of 3 or 5 can be discovered later; it is not part of initialization.
items.transfer: What should the source-to-source distance be even when S has no outgoing edges? Explain the role of the empty route.

items.prompt: C is unsettled with tentative distance 8 and an existing predecessor. B is now settled at distance 3. The directed edge B → C has weight 7. How should this relaxation update C?
options: Replace C by 7, the new edge’s weight
Keep C at 8 and keep its existing predecessor
Replace C by 10 and set its predecessor to B
Add 8 and 7 to record all routes into C
items.explanation: The route through B costs 3 + 7 = 10. It is worse than the existing route of cost 8, so neither the distance nor the predecessor changes. Relaxation compares candidate routes; it does not add competing route costs together.
items.transfer: What is the largest whole-number weight for B → C that would strictly improve the current distance 8? Check the strict inequality.

items.prompt: The unsettled vertices with discovered routes are A at tentative distance 6, B at 2, and C at 4. All edge weights are nonnegative. Which vertex should Dijkstra settle next?
options: B, because its tentative distance of 2 is the minimum
A, because its label comes first alphabetically
C, because its value lies between the other two
No vertex, because every remaining distance must first be equal
items.explanation: Dijkstra selects the unsettled vertex with the smallest current total distance from the source: B at 2. Labels are useful only for breaking equal-distance ties. The rule is not to pick a median value or wait for equal distances.
items.transfer: If A also had tentative distance 2, could settling A before B still be correct? Distinguish a tie policy from the shortest-path guarantee.

items.prompt: The only directed edges are S → T (9), S → A (2), A → B (1), and B → T (2). Settling S first discovers T at 9. In a target-only Dijkstra search with nonnegative weights, when is it safe to stop with a final distance for T?
options: As soon as the first outgoing edge reaches T
After visiting the vertex named immediately before T
When T is selected as the minimum and settled
When the direct S → T edge has been checked twice
items.explanation: Discovery is not settlement. A is next at 2, then B at 3, which improves T to 5. When T becomes the minimum unsettled discovered vertex and is settled, its distance is final. A target-only search can stop there; solving distances to every reachable vertex may continue.
items.transfer: After settling only S, give the displayed distance for T and say whether it is tentative or final. Then give its eventual final value.

items.prompt: The edges are S → A (2), S → B (2), A → T (3), and B → T (3). This trace breaks equal-distance vertex ties alphabetically and keeps the first predecessor when a new route has equal cost. After A sets T to 5, B is settled. What happens to T?
options: T becomes 2 because A and B have equal distances
T stays at 5; this trace keeps A as its predecessor
T becomes 10 because two different routes reach it
T must switch to B because B was processed more recently
items.explanation: B offers another route of cost 2 + 3 = 5. It is equally short, so the stated policy keeps T’s existing predecessor A. Both S → A → T and S → B → T are shortest routes. A reproducible tie choice does not make the other route incorrect.
items.transfer: If a different implementation kept B on equal cost, which result must still agree with this one: the predecessor, the distance, or both? Explain.

items.prompt: Consider a graph with only S → T (2), S → A (5), and A → T (−4). A Dijkstra variant stops when it settles T. Why does allowing this negative edge invalidate that stopping guarantee?
options: It must report 1 because negative edges are always examined first
It must report −4 because that is the lightest individual edge
It must declare T unreachable whenever a negative edge exists
It could report 2 even though S → A → T costs 1
items.explanation: After settling S, T has estimate 2 and A has estimate 5. Settling T next would stop at 2, but the route through A costs 5 − 4 = 1. The graph has no cycle; a negative cycle is not required for this failure. The explorer refuses negative weights instead of presenting Dijkstra’s result as guaranteed.
items.transfer: Why does adding the same positive constant to every edge fail as a general repair? Compare a one-edge route with a two-edge route.

items.prompt: A run starts at S in a graph containing only S → A (0) and A → B (2), plus an isolated vertex X. All reachable vertices have been settled and the frontier is empty. X has never received a finite distance. What does this mean?
options: X has cost 0 because no edge was traversed to reach it
X takes the largest finite distance already in the table
No directed path from S to X exists; X is unreachable
X must be removed before any other result can be read
items.explanation: Every discovered reachable vertex has been processed. No directed path from S reaches X, so X remains unreachable rather than receiving cost 0 or a copied finite value. Infinity or an explicit unreachable marker describes absence of a path; it is not an unusually large route cost.
items.transfer: How would the answer change if the edge B → X of weight 0 were added? Calculate X’s new distance.

items.prompt: Assume Dijkstra has correctly settled earlier vertices and every edge weight is nonnegative. U is the minimum unsettled vertex at distance 4. Which argument explains why a still-hidden route cannot later make U cheaper than 4?
options: A cheaper path would already have exposed a frontier estimate below 4 when it first left the settled set
All other tentative distances must already be final, so no later relaxation can improve any recorded route
The last edge used to reach U is the cheapest edge in the whole graph, so the complete path must be shortest
U cannot have an incoming edge from an unsettled vertex, because nonnegative graphs cannot contain cycles
items.explanation: Suppose a cheaper route existed. Follow it from S to the first unsettled vertex Y. Its predecessor X was already settled with a final distance, so processing X offered Y a route costing no more than that prefix. Nonnegative remaining edges make this prefix no greater than the supposedly cheaper full route. Y would therefore have an estimate below 4, contradicting the choice of U as the minimum.
items.transfer: Point to the step in this argument that fails when a remaining edge can have negative weight. Use the three-edge example S → T (2), S → A (5), A → T (−4).
